# Research operating manual — for the agent running on this box

You are an autonomous research agent running **headless on a cloud sandbox**:
4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk, **CPU-only — there is no GPU here**. Your job is to
carry a research task to a real, measured result, and to leave behind a record
good enough that a stranger can check your work.

Read this whole document before you act. Your specific mission is given
separately when you are launched.

## The machine you are on

- **CPU only.** Size every experiment to 4 vCPU / 8 GB. Small models, subsampled
  data, short runs. Do not go looking for a GPU. If a step genuinely needs one,
  record that as a finding and work around it.
- **Ephemeral.** This box can stop at any moment. Anything that exists only here
  is lost when it does. Push your work outward continuously.
- **One session.** You are a single headless session. You **cannot** schedule a
  wake-up, re-invoke yourself, or come back later. When this session ends,
  nothing resumes it.

That last point has a hard consequence: **stay in-session for the whole budget.**
Never background a long sweep and exit expecting to collect results later — those
results will be stranded. If a computation is long, run it in the foreground, or
launch it and poll it from *this same session*, harvesting each result as it
lands.

## How to do the work

1. **Orient before acting.** Read what already exists — your workspace, your
   notes, prior results. Do not redo work that is already done.
2. **Decide the next step and say why.** A step you cannot justify is a step you
   should not take.
3. **Run it.** Keep it CPU-sized. Write outputs — metrics, plots, logs — under
   `~/research/artifacts/`.
4. **Record what happened**, including when it did not work. See your memory
   system below.
5. **Push the code out** (see Publishing).
6. **Repeat**, preferring depth on a live thread over breadth across shallow ones.

## Discipline — these are the rules that make the result worth anything

- **Be honest.** Record failures, dead ends, and uncertainty. Never fabricate a
  number, never round a result toward what you hoped for, and never describe a
  run you did not do. A negative result recorded honestly is worth more than a
  positive one you cannot defend.
- **Measure, do not assert.** "It works" is not a result. The number is the
  result. State what you measured, on what data, with what settings.
- **Be reproducible.** Pin versions, seeds, and data references. Anyone
  re-running a step from your record must get your number back.
- **Report negative results.** A refuted hypothesis is a real finding. Write it
  down with the same care as a success.
- **Record dead ends, not just outcomes.** The fact that an approach *failed*,
  and why, is the most expensive knowledge you will produce. Losing it means the
  next person pays for it again.
- **Small, frequent steps.** Record as you go. Do not save it all for one dump at
  the end — the box may not give you an end.
- **Say what you are uncertain about.** Distinguish "I measured this" from "I
  believe this" from "I assumed this".

## Publishing — commit early, commit often, push every time

This box is ephemeral, so work that lives only here, or is committed locally but
never pushed, is **lost**. Publish continuously, not once at the end.

1. **Publish early.** As soon as you have a skeleton — one script and a stub
   README — create the repo and push:

       ~/research/bin/publish-repo <repo-name> [source-dir]

   Pick a descriptive kebab-case name. The helper creates a **public** repo under
   the configured owner and pushes `main`. Research is meant to be replicable, so
   it is public by design.

2. **Then commit and push after every meaningful step** — a working baseline,
   each result, each fix. From the repo directory:

       git add -A && git commit -m "<what changed>" && \
         git push "https://x-access-token:${GITHUB_TOKEN}@github.com/${GITHUB_OWNER}/<repo-name>.git" HEAD:main

3. **Keep the README current** with the latest finding and how to reproduce it.

4. **Keep the repo clean.** A `.gitignore` is created on first publish. Do not
   commit the seeded scaffolding (`CLAUDE.md`, `.env`, `.provisioned`, `bin/`),
   byte caches, or raw data dumps. **Do** commit `artifacts/` — the metrics
   behind each claim — so the repo stands alone.

Treat every push as a checkpoint: if the box died right now, everything you have
proven so far should already be pushed.

## Definition of done

Do not stop until all of these hold:

1. **Every claim you make is backed by a recorded number** you can point to.
2. **Every step you took is written down** — what you did, what happened, and
   what it means. A title is not a record.
3. **Your dead ends are written down too**, with what you learned from them.
4. **Your code is pushed to GitHub** and the repo URL appears in your record.
5. **Your final state is summarized**: what you found, what you did not resolve,
   and what a follow-up should try next.

If you are running low on budget, finish recording and pushing the work you have
already done before starting anything new. Unrecorded work is wasted work.

## Your memory system: Flywheel

Your memory is **Flywheel** — a graph-based system for tracking research work,
decisions, and evidence over time. Think "git for science": a DAG of research
**nodes** carrying ideas, plans, experiments, and the artifacts that back them
up. Record everything you do there, so your work is traceable and replicable by
anyone who reads the graph later.

Your interface is the **Flywheel MCP tools**, already wired into this session and
namespaced `mcp__flywheel__*`.

**Read the live contract first**, before anything else — it is self-describing
and always current:

- `flywheel_get_contract` — the operation catalog and node model.
- `flywheel_get_contract_section` — deep dives, in this order: `graph` →
  `stage_commit` → `artifacts` → `sharing`.

If this document ever disagrees with the contract, **the contract wins**.

### The unit of record: a node

A node is one unit of research. Its body is exactly three fields:

- **`title`** — a short, specific, self-describing line (~60–80 chars).
- **`content`** — the substance, in Markdown. A reliable skeleton is
  **Hypothesis → Setup → Results (with deltas vs the baseline) → Interpretation**.
  Dense, about 1k chars, not an essay.
- **`summary`** — 1–3 sentences stating the concrete change **relative to this
  node's parent** and the outcome, so a reader can follow the step from the text
  alone. Include a verdict: GREEN / RED / REFUTED.

Do **not** write typed fields like `kind`, `node_type`, or `hypothesis` — they
were removed and the server rejects them. Whether a node is an idea, a plan, or
an experiment is conveyed in your prose.

Two kinds of node are both first-class. **Insight nodes** — an observation, a
plan, a decision and its rationale, a branch point, a synthesis — legitimately
have no artifacts, and that is correct. **Empirical nodes** — a concrete run with
a measured outcome — **must** carry at least one finalized artifact.

### Structure: build a graph, not a chain

The most common failure is a flat linear chain, each node the sole child of the
last. That throws away the point of the system. Encode the **real causal
structure** of your research:

- **`flywheel_commit_new_node`** — create a node. `parent_ids` is what it
  genuinely builds on, and it can be more than one.
- **`flywheel_branch_node`** — fork an alternative line of inquiry. Explore
  option A versus option B by branching twice from the same parent, so they sit
  side by side.
- **`flywheel_merge_nodes`** / **`flywheel_add_parent`** — reconcile threads, and
  cross-link a node to all of its real lineage. This is what makes it a DAG.

The shape that works: a **shallow trunk that branches wide into experiment
leaves, with periodic synthesis nodes that merge siblings**. When your next step
builds on an earlier hub rather than the last thing you ran, parent it on the
hub. Merge to **synthesize, not to collect** — every merge must state what the
combination *means*.

Use **tags** to keep a growing graph legible: define a tag once on the root
(`flywheel_create_node_tag`), then assign (`flywheel_set_node_tag_assignments`)
along `Cluster: <family>`, `outcome:GREEN|RED`, and `kind:…`.

### The loop you run

1. **Orient.** Read the contract, then traverse the DAG around your target:
   `flywheel_list_nodes` (`owners:["me"]`), `flywheel_get_node`,
   `flywheel_get_node_children` / `_parents` / `_tree`.
2. **Frame the step as a node** — insight or empirical — and decide its parents.
3. **Run it**, writing outputs under `~/research/artifacts/`.
4. **Attach artifacts before you commit an empirical node.** Three calls:
   `flywheel_prepare_artifact_uploads` → HTTP **PUT** the raw bytes to the
   returned `upload_url` with the returned headers (expect **202**) →
   `flywheel_finalize_artifact_uploads`. Attach the metrics and a `run.json`
   recording the exact command, environment, and seeds.
5. **Commit** with `flywheel_commit_new_node`.
6. **Make it public** — `flywheel_set_sharing_for_nodes`, `sharing_mode: public`.
   New nodes are not public by default.
7. **Verify, then iterate.** Re-read the node; confirm the artifact count is
   non-zero and the body is written.

To **edit** an existing node: `flywheel_get_node` (note its `revision`) →
`flywheel_acquire_stage_lease` → `flywheel_commit_node` with
`base_committed_revision`. On a `409`, re-read and retry.

### Rules

- **Empirical nodes are never empty.** Zero artifacts is a failed unit of work
  even if the code ran. Insight nodes correctly have none.
- **Every node has a written body.** A title is not enough.
- **Build a graph.** Real parents, branches for alternatives, synthesis nodes.
- **Everything public.** A private node is invisible and does not count.
- **Commit as you go** — one node per coherent step, not one dump at the end.
- **Record negative results as nodes.** A refuted hypothesis is a valid node.
- **Stop cleanly**: finish with a multi-parent synthesis node saying what you
  found and what a follow-up should try.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Word2Vec skip-gram with negative sampling, from scratch.
Implements the method from:
  Mikolov et al. (2013), "Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space"
  Mikolov et al. (2013), "Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality"

Uses Numba for CPU-accelerated training on a single box without a GPU.
"""

import argparse
import json
import math
import os
import random
import time
import zipfile
from collections import Counter

import numpy as np
from numba import njit, prange
from tqdm import tqdm


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data loading
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def load_text8(path="text8"):
    """Load the text8 corpus as a list of tokens."""
    if path.endswith(".zip"):
        with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as zf:
            name = zf.namelist()[0]
            text = zf.read(name).decode("utf-8")
    else:
        with open(path) as f:
            text = f.read()
    return text.split()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Vocabulary building
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def build_vocab(tokens, min_count=5):
    """
    Build vocabulary from tokens.
    Returns word2id, id2word, word_counts, and filtered tokens (as ints).
    """
    counter = Counter(tokens)
    # Filter by min_count
    vocab = [w for w, c in counter.items() if c >= min_count]
    word2id = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
    id2word = {i: w for w, i in word2id.items()}
    word_counts = np.array([counter[w] for w in vocab], dtype=np.int64)
    # Convert tokens to ids, dropping OOV words
    token_ids = np.array(
        [word2id[t] for t in tokens if t in word2id], dtype=np.int32
    )
    return word2id, id2word, word_counts, token_ids


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Negative sampling noise distribution (unigram ^ 0.75)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def build_noise_distribution(word_counts):
    """Build the negative sampling noise distribution: p(w) ∝ count(w)^0.75."""
    freqs = word_counts.astype(np.float64) ** 0.75
    freqs /= freqs.sum()
    return freqs


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Subsampling table
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def build_subsample_probs(word_counts, threshold=1e-5):
    """
    Compute subsampling probability for each word.
    P(drop) = 1 - sqrt(threshold / freq) for words above the threshold.
    """
    total = word_counts.sum()
    freqs = word_counts.astype(np.float64) / total
    drop_probs = np.maximum(0.0, 1.0 - np.sqrt(threshold / freqs))
    return drop_probs


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training — Numba-accelerated core
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@njit(nogil=True, fastmath=True, cache=True)
def _train_sg_neg_epoch(
    token_ids,
    word_counts,
    noise_pow,
    W_in,
    W_out,
    lr_start,
    lr_end,
    window,
    neg_samples,
    subsample_threshold,
    seed,
):
    """
    One epoch of skip-gram negative sampling.
    Updates W_in and W_out in-place.

    Parameters
    ----------
    token_ids: int32[n_tokens] — sentence-concatenated token IDs
    word_counts: int64[vocab_size]
    noise_pow: float64[vocab_size] — unigram^0.75 distribution (unnormalized OK, but should sum~1)
    W_in: float32[vocab_size, dim]
    W_out: float32[vocab_size, dim]
    lr_start, lr_end: linear LR schedule
    window: int
    neg_samples: int
    subsample_threshold: float — the threshold t (e.g., 1e-5)
    seed: int
    """
    vocab_size, dim = W_in.shape
    n_tokens = len(token_ids)
    total = word_counts.sum()

    # Build subsampling drop probabilities
    freqs = word_counts / total
    drop_probs = np.maximum(np.float64(0.0), 1.0 - np.sqrt(subsample_threshold / freqs))
    # threshold so we know which words are frequent enough to subsample at all
    # Pre-computed noise cumulative distribution for fast sampling
    noise_cumsum = np.cumsum(noise_pow)

    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)

    # For each position in the corpus
    for pos in range(n_tokens):
        word = token_ids[pos]
        # Subsampling: skip frequent words probabilistically
        if drop_probs[word] > 0.0 and rng.random_sample() < drop_probs[word]:
            continue

        # Linear learning rate decay
        lr = lr_start + (lr_end - lr_start) * (pos / n_tokens)

        # Determine the dynamic window
        dyn_window = rng.randint(1, window + 1)

        # Context window around the word
        start = max(0, pos - dyn_window)
        end = min(n_tokens, pos + dyn_window + 1)

        for ctx_pos in range(start, end):
            if ctx_pos == pos:
                continue
            ctx_word = token_ids[ctx_pos]

            # --- Positive sample (ctx_word) ---
            # Compute dot product: W_in[word] · W_out[ctx_word]
            dot = np.float32(0.0)
            for d in range(dim):
                dot += W_in[word, d] * W_out[ctx_word, d]
            score = np.float32(1.0) / (np.float32(1.0) + np.exp(-dot))

            # Gradient for positive: (label - score) = (1 - score)
            g_pos = np.float32(1.0) - score
            g_pos_lr = g_pos * lr

            # Update W_in[word] and W_out[ctx_word]
            for d in range(dim):
                w_in_grad = g_pos_lr * W_out[ctx_word, d]
                w_out_grad = g_pos_lr * W_in[word, d]
                W_in[word, d] += w_in_grad
                W_out[ctx_word, d] += w_out_grad

            # --- Negative samples ---
            for _ in range(neg_samples):
                # Sample a negative word from noise distribution
                r = rng.random_sample()
                neg_word = 0
                # Linear scan of cumsum — O(V) but V is ~100k
                # This is a bottleneck; we'll use alias sampling in production
                for j in range(vocab_size):
                    if noise_cumsum[j] >= r:
                        neg_word = j
                        break

                if neg_word == ctx_word:
                    continue  # skip if it collides with the positive context

                dot_neg = np.float32(0.0)
                for d in range(dim):
                    dot_neg += W_in[word, d] * W_out[neg_word, d]
                score_neg = np.float32(1.0) / (np.float32(1.0) + np.exp(-dot_neg))

                # Gradient for negative: (0 - score_neg) = -score_neg
                g_neg = -score_neg
                g_neg_lr = g_neg * lr

                for d in range(dim):
                    w_in_grad = g_neg_lr * W_out[neg_word, d]
                    w_out_grad = g_neg_lr * W_in[word, d]
                    W_in[word, d] += w_in_grad
                    W_out[neg_word, d] += w_out_grad


@njit(nogil=True, inline='always')
def _binary_search_cumsum(noise_cumsum, r):
    """Binary search on cumsum: find first index where cumsum >= r."""
    lo = 0
    hi = len(noise_cumsum) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if noise_cumsum[mid] < r:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo


@njit(nogil=True)
def _train_sg_neg_epoch_v2(
    token_ids,
    word_counts,
    noise_cumsum,
    W_in,
    W_out,
    lr_start,
    lr_end,
    window,
    neg_samples,
    subsample_threshold,
    seed,
):
    """
    Optimized skip-gram epoch: inlines binary search, clips dot products.
    Correct gradient: for both positive and negative samples, use the
    original (pre-update) w_in[d] to compute both gradient contributions.
    """
    vocab_size, dim = W_in.shape
    n_tokens = len(token_ids)
    MAX_DOT = np.float32(15.0)   # exp(15) ≈ 3.3e6, safe for float32
    MIN_DOT = np.float32(-15.0)

    total = np.float64(word_counts.sum())
    freqs = word_counts.astype(np.float64) / total
    drop_probs = np.maximum(np.float64(0.0), 1.0 - np.sqrt(subsample_threshold / freqs))

    np.random.seed(seed)

    for pos in range(n_tokens):
        word = token_ids[pos]
        if drop_probs[word] > np.float64(0.0) and np.random.random_sample() < drop_probs[word]:
            continue

        lr = lr_start + (lr_end - lr_start) * (np.float64(pos) / np.float64(n_tokens))
        lr_f32 = np.float32(lr)
        dyn_window = np.random.randint(1, window + 1)
        start = max(0, pos - dyn_window)
        end = min(n_tokens, pos + dyn_window + 1)

        w_in_word = W_in[word]

        for ctx_pos in range(start, end):
            if ctx_pos == pos:
                continue
            ctx_word = token_ids[ctx_pos]
            w_out_ctx = W_out[ctx_word]

            # --- Positive sample ---
            dot = np.float32(0.0)
            for d in range(dim):
                dot += w_in_word[d] * w_out_ctx[d]
            if dot > MAX_DOT:
                dot = MAX_DOT
            elif dot < MIN_DOT:
                dot = MIN_DOT
            score = np.float32(1.0) / (np.float32(1.0) + np.exp(-dot))
            g = (np.float32(1.0) - score) * lr_f32
            for d in range(dim):
                w_in_old = w_in_word[d]
                w_out_old = w_out_ctx[d]
                w_in_word[d] = w_in_old + g * w_out_old
                w_out_ctx[d] = w_out_old + g * w_in_old

            # --- Negative samples ---
            for _ in range(neg_samples):
                r = np.random.random_sample()
                lo = 0
                hi = vocab_size - 1
                while lo < hi:
                    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
                    if noise_cumsum[mid] < r:
                        lo = mid + 1
                    else:
                        hi = mid
                neg_word = lo
                if neg_word == ctx_word:
                    continue

                w_out_neg = W_out[neg_word]
                dot_neg = np.float32(0.0)
                for d in range(dim):
                    dot_neg += w_in_word[d] * w_out_neg[d]
                if dot_neg > MAX_DOT:
                    dot_neg = MAX_DOT
                elif dot_neg < MIN_DOT:
                    dot_neg = MIN_DOT
                score_neg = np.float32(1.0) / (np.float32(1.0) + np.exp(-dot_neg))
                g_neg = (-score_neg) * lr_f32
                for d in range(dim):
                    w_in_old = w_in_word[d]
                    w_out_neg_old = w_out_neg[d]
                    w_in_word[d] = w_in_old + g_neg * w_out_neg_old
                    w_out_neg[d] = w_out_neg_old + g_neg * w_in_old


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training — high-level driver
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def train(
    token_ids,
    word_counts,
    dim=100,
    window=5,
    neg_samples=5,
    subsample_threshold=1e-5,
    lr=0.025,
    epochs=3,
    seed=42,
):
    """
    Train word2vec skip-gram with negative sampling.
    """
    vocab_size = len(word_counts)
    n_tokens = len(token_ids)

    print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size}")
    print(f"Corpus tokens (after min_count filter): {n_tokens:,}")
    print(f"Training with dim={dim}, window={window}, neg={neg_samples}, "
          f"epochs={epochs}, lr={lr}, subsample_t={subsample_threshold}, seed={seed}")

    # Initialize weights: small random values
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    W_in = rng.randn(vocab_size, dim).astype(np.float32) * 0.01
    W_out = rng.randn(vocab_size, dim).astype(np.float32) * 0.01

    # Noise distribution
    noise = build_noise_distribution(word_counts)
    noise_cumsum = np.cumsum(noise)

    t0 = time.time()

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        lr_start = lr * (1.0 - epoch / epochs)
        lr_end = lr_start * 0.01
        epoch_seed = seed + epoch * 1000

        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}: lr {lr_start:.6f} → {lr_end:.6f}")

        _train_sg_neg_epoch_v2(
            token_ids,
            word_counts,
            noise_cumsum,
            W_in,
            W_out,
            lr_start,
            lr_end,
            window,
            neg_samples,
            subsample_threshold,
            epoch_seed,
        )

        elapsed = time.time() - t0
        print(f"  elapsed: {elapsed:.1f}s")

    training_time = time.time() - t0
    print(f"Total training time: {training_time:.1f}s")

    # Combine W_in and W_out — common practice that often improves results
    vectors = W_in + W_out
    return vectors, W_out, training_time


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Evaluation: word analogies
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def load_analogies(path):
    """Parse questions-words.txt into sections and question tuples."""
    sections = {}
    current_section = None
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            if line.startswith(":"):
                current_section = line[1:].strip()
                sections[current_section] = []
            else:
                parts = line.split()
                if len(parts) == 4:
                    sections[current_section].append(
                        (parts[0].lower(), parts[1].lower(),
                         parts[2].lower(), parts[3].lower())
                    )
    return sections


def evaluate_analogies(vectors, word2id, id2word, sections, dim):
    """
    Evaluate word analogies using 3CosAdd: argmax cos(v_b - v_a + v_c, v_d).
    Exclude a, b, c from candidates.
    Returns total correct, total asked, per-section stats, and skip count.
    """
    # Normalize all vectors
    norms = np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    norms[norms == 0] = 1.0
    vectors_norm = vectors / norms

    # Precompute all-vs-all similarity? No, we'll do it per query (vocab ~100k, dim ~100)
    # For efficiency, we can compute the query and do a single matrix multiply
    # query_vec: (1, dim), dot with (vocab, dim).T → (1, vocab)

    semantic_sections = {
        "capital-common-countries", "capital-world", "currency",
        "city-in-state", "family", "gram1-adjective-to-adverb",
        "gram2-opposite", "gram3-comparative", "gram4-superlative",
        "gram5-present-participle", "gram6-nationality-adjective",
        "gram7-past-tense", "gram8-plural", "gram9-plural-verbs",
    }
    # Semantic sections are the first 5 in the standard file
    semantic_set = {
        "capital-common-countries", "capital-world", "currency",
        "city-in-state", "family",
    }

    total_correct = 0
    total_asked = 0
    total_skipped = 0
    section_results = {}

    for section_name, questions in sections.items():
        correct = 0
        asked = 0
        skipped = 0

        for a, b, c, d_true in questions:
            # Check all words are in vocabulary
            if a not in word2id or b not in word2id or c not in word2id or d_true not in word2id:
                skipped += 1
                continue

            id_a = word2id[a]
            id_b = word2id[b]
            id_c = word2id[c]
            id_d_true = word2id[d_true]

            # Compute query: v_b - v_a + v_c
            query = vectors_norm[id_b] - vectors_norm[id_a] + vectors_norm[id_c]

            # Dot product with all words
            scores = np.dot(vectors_norm, query)

            # Exclude a, b, c
            scores[id_a] = -np.inf
            scores[id_b] = -np.inf
            scores[id_c] = -np.inf

            pred_id = np.argmax(scores)
            asked += 1
            if pred_id == id_d_true:
                correct += 1

        if asked > 0:
            section_results[section_name] = {
                "correct": correct,
                "asked": asked,
                "skipped": skipped,
                "accuracy": correct / asked,
            }
            total_correct += correct
            total_asked += asked
            total_skipped += skipped

    # Separate semantic and syntactic
    semantic_correct = sum(
        section_results[s]["correct"]
        for s in section_results if s in semantic_set
    )
    semantic_asked = sum(
        section_results[s]["asked"]
        for s in section_results if s in semantic_set
    )
    syntactic_correct = total_correct - semantic_correct
    syntactic_asked = total_asked - semantic_asked

    return {
        "total": {
            "correct": total_correct,
            "asked": total_asked,
            "skipped": total_skipped,
            "accuracy": total_correct / total_asked if total_asked > 0 else 0.0,
        },
        "semantic": {
            "correct": semantic_correct,
            "asked": semantic_asked,
            "accuracy": semantic_correct / semantic_asked if semantic_asked > 0 else 0.0,
        },
        "syntactic": {
            "correct": syntactic_correct,
            "asked": syntactic_asked,
            "accuracy": syntactic_correct / syntactic_asked if syntactic_asked > 0 else 0.0,
        },
        "sections": section_results,
    }


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Save vectors in word2vec text format
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def save_vectors(path, vectors, id2word):
    """Save vectors in word2vec text format."""
    vocab_size, dim = vectors.shape
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write(f"{vocab_size} {dim}\n")
        for i in range(vocab_size):
            word = id2word[i]
            vec_str = " ".join(f"{v:.6f}" for v in vectors[i])
            f.write(f"{word} {vec_str}\n")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Train word2vec skip-gram on text8")
    parser.add_argument("--text8", default="text8")
    parser.add_argument("--questions", default="questions-words.txt")
    parser.add_argument("--dim", type=int, default=100)
    parser.add_argument("--window", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--neg", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=3)
    parser.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=0.025)
    parser.add_argument("--subsample", type=float, default=1e-5)
    parser.add_argument("--min-count", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    parser.add_argument("--output-vectors", default="artifacts/vectors.txt")
    parser.add_argument("--output-results", default="artifacts/results.json")
    parser.add_argument("--quick", action="store_true",
                        help="Quick test with tiny settings")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.quick:
        args.dim = 50
        args.epochs = 1
        args.window = 2
        args.neg = 2
        print("QUICK MODE — tiny model for testing")

    # Load data
    print("Loading text8...")
    tokens = load_text8(args.text8)
    print(f"Raw tokens: {len(tokens):,}")

    # Build vocabulary
    print("Building vocabulary...")
    word2id, id2word, word_counts, token_ids = build_vocab(tokens, args.min_count)

    # Train
    vectors, W_out, training_time = train(
        token_ids,
        word_counts,
        dim=args.dim,
        window=args.window,
        neg_samples=args.neg,
        subsample_threshold=args.subsample,
        lr=args.lr,
        epochs=args.epochs,
        seed=args.seed,
    )

    # We use W_in as the final word vectors (standard choice)
    # Some use W_in + W_out; we use W_in for simplicity

    # Evaluate
    print("\nEvaluating analogies...")
    sections = load_analogies(args.questions)
    results = evaluate_analogies(vectors, word2id, id2word, sections, args.dim)

    print(f"\nTotal accuracy: {results['total']['accuracy']:.4f} "
          f"({results['total']['correct']}/{results['total']['asked']})")
    print(f"  Skipped: {results['total']['skipped']}")
    print(f"Semantic: {results['semantic']['accuracy']:.4f} "
          f"({results['semantic']['correct']}/{results['semantic']['asked']})")
    print(f"Syntactic: {results['syntactic']['accuracy']:.4f} "
          f"({results['syntactic']['correct']}/{results['syntactic']['asked']})")

    # Save vectors
    os.makedirs("artifacts", exist_ok=True)
    save_vectors(args.output_vectors, vectors, id2word)
    print(f"\nVectors saved to {args.output_vectors}")

    # Save results
    results_json = {
        "hyperparameters": {
            "dim": args.dim,
            "window": args.window,
            "negative_samples": args.neg,
            "epochs": args.epochs,
            "subsampling_threshold": args.subsample,
            "learning_rate": args.lr,
            "min_count": args.min_count,
            "seed": args.seed,
            "training_time_seconds": round(training_time, 1),
        },
        "vocabulary_size": len(word2id),
        "corpus_tokens_after_filter": int(len(token_ids)),
        "accuracy": results["total"]["accuracy"],
        "semantic_accuracy": results["semantic"]["accuracy"],
        "syntactic_accuracy": results["syntactic"]["accuracy"],
        "total_correct": results["total"]["correct"],
        "total_asked": results["total"]["asked"],
        "total_skipped": results["total"]["skipped"],
        "section_details": results["sections"],
    }
    with open(args.output_results, "w") as f:
        json.dump(results_json, f, indent=2)
    print(f"Results saved to {args.output_results}")

staged_payload.title: Exp01 — dim=200, neg=15, epochs=5: Analogy accuracy 17.11% (GREEN baseline)
staged_payload.content:
## Hypothesis

A dim=200 model with 15 negative samples and 5 epochs should achieve reasonable analogy performance on text8 — targeting >15% on the word analogy benchmark, competitive with published CPU-trained text8 results.

## Setup

- **Corpus**: text8 (100MB, 16.7M tokens after min_count=5 filter)
- **Vocabulary**: 71,290 words
- **Architecture**: Skip-gram with negative sampling (Numba-accelerated v2)
- **Hyperparameters**: dim=200, window=5, neg=15, epochs=5, lr=0.025, subsample_t=1e-5, min_count=5, seed=42
- **Vector combination**: W_in + W_out (current code default)
- **Evaluation**: 3CosAdd on Google word analogy dataset (19,544 questions, 1,717 skipped as OOV)
- **Training time**: 953.8s (~15.9 min) on 4 vCPU

## Results

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total accuracy | 17.11% (3,051/17,827) |
| Semantic accuracy | 11.60% |
| Syntactic accuracy | 21.05% |
| Skipped (OOV) | 1,717 |

**Top sections**: family (42.1%), gram3-comparative (41.7%), gram6-nationality (35.4%), capital-common-countries (30.8%)

**Bottom sections**: gram2-opposite (5.4%), currency (6.7%), gram1-adjective-to-adverb (7.4%), capital-world (7.7%)

## Interpretation

17.1% accuracy on the analogy task is below published text8 results (typically 20-35%), but this is a working from-scratch implementation. The syntactic accuracy (21.1%) substantially outperforms semantic (11.6%), which is expected for a pure distributional model on a small corpus — syntactic relationships (plural, past tense) are more local and frequent.

Key limitation: code uses W_in + W_out as final vectors, which may not be optimal. Standard practice uses W_in only.

## Hypothesis

A faster training configuration (only 3 epochs, 5 negative samples) should still produce usable embeddings, though with lower accuracy than the 5-epoch/15-neg run.

## Setup

- Same corpus, vocabulary, and architecture as Exp01
- **Hyperparameters**: dim=200, window=5, neg=5, epochs=3, lr=0.025, subsample_t=1e-5, min_count=5, seed=42
- **Vector combination**: W_in + W_out
- **Training time**: 209.6s (~3.5 min)

## Results

| Metric | Value | vs Exp01 (neg=15, ep=5) |
|--------|-------|--------------------------|
| Total accuracy | 10.66% (1,900/17,827) | -6.45pp |
| Semantic accuracy | 6.31% | -5.29pp |
| Syntactic accuracy | 13.75% | -7.29pp |
| Skipped (OOV) | 1,717 | same |

## Interpretation

Reducing from 5→3 epochs and 15→5 negative samples drops accuracy by 6.5 percentage points (10.66% vs 17.11%). The degradation is substantial, especially in syntactic accuracy (-7.3pp). This confirms that both more epochs and more negative samples are important for quality.

Training time scales roughly linearly: 210s for 3 epochs vs 954s for 5 epochs (factor 4.5x time for 1.6x accuracy gain). This is a meaningful CPU budget tradeoff.

node.title: Exp01 — dim=200, neg=15, epochs=5: Analogy accuracy 17.11% (GREEN baseline)
node.content:
## Hypothesis

A dim=200 model with 15 negative samples and 5 epochs should achieve reasonable analogy performance on text8 — targeting >15% on the word analogy benchmark, competitive with published CPU-trained text8 results.

## Setup

- **Corpus**: text8 (100MB, 16.7M tokens after min_count=5 filter)
- **Vocabulary**: 71,290 words
- **Architecture**: Skip-gram with negative sampling (Numba-accelerated v2)
- **Hyperparameters**: dim=200, window=5, neg=15, epochs=5, lr=0.025, subsample_t=1e-5, min_count=5, seed=42
- **Vector combination**: W_in + W_out (current code default)
- **Evaluation**: 3CosAdd on Google word analogy dataset (19,544 questions, 1,717 skipped as OOV)
- **Training time**: 953.8s (~15.9 min) on 4 vCPU

## Results

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total accuracy | 17.11% (3,051/17,827) |
| Semantic accuracy | 11.60% |
| Syntactic accuracy | 21.05% |
| Skipped (OOV) | 1,717 |

**Top sections**: family (42.1%), gram3-comparative (41.7%), gram6-nationality (35.4%), capital-common-countries (30.8%)

**Bottom sections**: gram2-opposite (5.4%), currency (6.7%), gram1-adjective-to-adverb (7.4%), capital-world (7.7%)

## Interpretation

17.1% accuracy on the analogy task is below published text8 results (typically 20-35%), but this is a working from-scratch implementation. The syntactic accuracy (21.1%) substantially outperforms semantic (11.6%), which is expected for a pure distributional model on a small corpus — syntactic relationships (plural, past tense) are more local and frequent.

Key limitation: code uses W_in + W_out as final vectors, which may not be optimal. Standard practice uses W_in only.
